definition: Structural subordination describes a conglomerate that operates through multiple organizational layers, such that in bankruptcy each subsidiary pays its own creditors first, and only leftover value flows up to the parent company.
core_idea: Creditors that extend credit at the parent level sit behind each subsidiary's own creditors in priority of repayment, making parent-level credit exposure inherently weaker than exposure to the operating subsidiary itself.
key_points: Each subsidiary settles its own creditors first out of its own assets before any residual value passes up to the parent.
Anyone holding credit exposure to the parent company has a low priority claim on assets that are actually owned by a subsidiary.
relationships: Contrasts with cross-guarantee structures and with Ring Fencing
trading_implications: Extending credit to a parent holding company (rather than the operating subsidiary that actually generates cash flow) carries structurally weaker repayment priority in a bankruptcy.
caveats: Treating exposure to the parent company as equivalent to exposure to the operating subsidiary — the parent's claim on subsidiary assets is subordinate to the subsidiary's own creditors.
